Endemic

/en-DEM-ik/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Endemic means native to, and found characteristically only in, one particular place or region.

The blind cave salamander is endemic to a single limestone spring in the Dinaric karst.

Worked Example

A botanist's survey of a Pacific archipelago lists 700 islands and one shrub with waxy, notched leaves. That shrub grows on twelve square kilometres of a single volcanic slope on one island and, after forty years of searching, on no other island in the chain and nowhere else on earth. Seeds planted elsewhere in the archipelago die within a season. The shrub is endemic to that one slope.

A species restricted to twelve square kilometres of one island out of 700, and found nowhere else on earth, has exactly the narrow, place-bound distribution that endemic names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

homegrown: Homegrown describes what sprang up in the place itself rather than being imported -- homegrown talent, homegrown produce. Endemic is the biologist's far stronger claim: not just from here, but found here and nowhere else on earth.

local: Local means found in or belonging to the immediate area, the way a local bakery or a local bird is simply one you meet nearby. Every one of a region's species is local to it when you are in that region; endemic claims a species is found in that one place and no other.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

introduced: brought in from somewhere else

cosmopolitan: found widely across many regions

Where it sits · how tightly tied to one place — native → endemic → exclusive

native vs. endemic: Native says only that a species arose where it now lives, while endemic adds that it lives nowhere else.

exclusive vs. endemic: Exclusive is the strongest way to put the same idea, and an endemic species is exclusive to its range by definition, which is why 'endemic to' is always followed by a place.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-

Prefix — en-: in, within (Greek)

Root — dem-

Root — dem-: people, district (Greek demos)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: of the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Greek demos meant both a people and the district they lived in, which is why democracy is rule by the people. Endemos meant 'in the district,' at home in one place and not elsewhere, and biology borrowed it for species that occur nowhere else. The same demos travels through epidemic, pandemic, and demographic.

Use the root in a new word: epidemic

Use the root in a new word: epidemic: An epidemic spreads 'among the people' (epi- plus demos), and endemic uses that same demos to mean 'in one district only.'

Root Check

Word Choice

scientific and technical

Endemic is nearly always followed by 'to' plus a place, and its whole force is the restriction: found here and nowhere else. Indigenous, among this unit's secondary words, is the broader term, meaning simply native to a place and used of peoples as well as species, without the found-nowhere-else claim that endemic makes.
